mainTopic: The ten conditions יהושע set when he divided ארץ ישראל, and the גמרא's explanation of the limits on the first several of them
overview: This amud opens in the middle of a ברייתא that lists the ten conditions יהושע set when he divided the land among the tribes. These conditions give the public small rights on private land. Examples are grazing animals, gathering wood and grasses, cutting shoots, drawing water, fishing, walking on paths, and burying a מת מצוה where it is found. The גמרא then goes through the conditions one at a time. רב פפא limits grazing to small animals in a forest of big trees. A chain of limits narrows the wood-gathering right: only thorns and shrubs, only while attached, only while moist, and never uprooting them. On grasses in a תלתן field, the גמרא raises a contradiction from a משנה in כלאים. It answers in two ways: seed versus stalks (רב ירמיה), or food for people versus animal feed, which רב פפא says you can tell by whether the field was planted in rows. Finally, an elder begins to explain exactly how shoots may be cut from olives, reeds, vines and other trees, and his list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The first six of יהושע's conditions
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא lists conditions that let the public use private land: grazing in forests, gathering wood, gathering wild grasses (except fenugreek), cutting shoots (except olive shoots), drawing water from a new spring, and fishing in ים טבריה without blocking boats.
steps.simpleTranslation: The conditions are that people may graze animals in forests, gather wood in others' fields, and gather grasses anywhere except a field of fenugreek. They may cut off shoots anywhere except olive shoots. The townspeople may draw water from a spring, even a brand-new one. People may fish in ים טבריה, as long as the fisherman does not spread a barrier that blocks the boats.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is listing the rights יהושע gave the public when he divided the land among the tribes. Each one is a small use of someone else's property that everyone is allowed to make.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you may not use another person's land or what grows on it. These conditions were built into the original division of the land, so owners received their land on the understanding that these uses are allowed. Notice the built-in limits: fenugreek, olive shoots, and blocking boats are excluded because those would cause the owner or the public real loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Fenugreek, a valuable crop that may not be taken
A barrier or net spread out in the water

phrases.english: That people may graze their animals in forests;
phrases.notes: This is in the middle of the list of יהושע's ten conditions. Even a privately owned forest is included.

phrases.english: and they may gather wood in their fields;
phrases.notes: "Their fields" means other people's fields, not your own.

phrases.english: and they may gather grasses in any place,
except from a fenugreek field;
and they may cut off shoots in any place,
except for olive shoots;
and a spring that comes out for the first time,
the people of the town may draw water from it;
and they may fish in the Sea of Tiberias,
provided that he does not spread out a barrier
and so hold up the boats;

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The public has fixed rights on private land: grazing in forests, gathering wood and grasses (except fenugreek), cutting shoots (except olive), drawing water from a spring, and fishing in ים טבריה without blocking boats.

steps.title: The remaining conditions of יהושע
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes the list: relieving oneself behind a fence, walking on private paths until the second rain, stepping off a damaged road onto the side, cutting through vineyards when lost, and burying a מת מצוה where it is found.
steps.simpleTranslation: People may relieve themselves behind a fence, even in a field full of saffron. They may walk on paths through private fields until the second rainfall. They may move to the sides of the roads because of hard bumps in the road. Someone lost among vineyards may cut branches to go up and cut branches to go down. A מת מצוה acquires the place where it lies.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues and completes the list of יהושע's conditions. These rights deal with privacy, walking, travel, getting lost, and burying an unattended body.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These rights cover real needs of people moving around the land. Each comes with a natural limit, such as walking on paths only until the second rain, when crops start to grow and walking would harm them. The last rule, that a מת מצוה is buried right where it is found, shows how highly the honor of the dead is valued, even over the owner's use of his field.

keyTerms.meaning: The second rainfall of the season
Hard bumps or ridges in the road
Cuts branches to clear a way through
A dead body with no one else to bury it

phrases.english: And they may relieve themselves behind a fence,
even in a field full of saffron;
and they may walk on the paths through private property,
until the second rainfall comes down;
and they may move off to the sides of the roads
because of hard bumps in the roads;
and one who gets lost among the vineyards
may cut branches and go up, cut branches and go down;
phrases.notes: He may clear a way through the vines in any direction until he finds the road again.

phrases.english: and a corpse with no one to bury it acquires its place.
phrases.notes: The body is buried right where it was found, even on someone's private land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and completes the same list of conditions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The public may also relieve themselves behind fences, walk private paths until the second rain, step off damaged roads, cut through vineyards when lost, and bury a מת מצוה where it lies.
steps.whatToRemember: יהושע built ten public rights into the division of the land. Each right lets people use private property in a way that does the owner little or no harm, and most come with a limit.

steps.title: רב פפא limits the right to graze in forests
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says the grazing right applies only to small animals in a forest of big trees. Small animals among small growth, or big animals among big trees, are not allowed, and big animals among small growth certainly are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the rule that people may graze animals in forests, רב פפא said: We said this only for small animals in a forest of big trees. But small animals in small growth, or big animals in big trees, are not allowed. And all the more so, big animals in small growth are not allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to the first condition and explains it. רב פפא narrows the grazing right to the one case where the forest is not harmed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sheep and goats cannot damage tall trees, so the owner loses nothing. Small animals would eat up young, low growth, and large animals like oxen can damage even big trees, so those cases are forbidden. If each of those is forbidden, then large animals in small growth, which does the most damage, is surely forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: We only said this about... (a phrase that limits a rule)
Small animals (like sheep and goats), or small growth
Large animals (like oxen), or large trees

steps.confusionAlert: The same words דקה and גסה describe both the animals and the trees. The first word is always the animal and the second is always the forest: דקה בגסה means small animals in a forest of big trees.

phrases.english: "That people may graze their animals in forests."
Rav Pappa said:
We said this only about small animals in a forest of big trees,
but small animals among small growth
and big animals among big trees, no.
And all the more so big animals among small growth, which is not allowed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא דַּקָּה בְּגַסָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the full list, the גמרא returns to the first item to explain its limits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Grazing in forests is allowed only for small animals in a forest of large trees; any combination that damages the forest is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the guiding idea behind all these conditions: the public right only goes as far as it causes the owner no real loss.

steps.title: Gathering wood means only thorns and shrubs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא limits the right to gather wood from others' fields to thorns and shrubs, which owners do not care about. Other kinds of wood may not be taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the rule that people may gather wood from others' fields: We said this only about thorns and shrubs, but other kinds of wood, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the second condition on the list and starts to narrow it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא just said "wood," which could sound like any wood at all. The גמרא explains it means only thorns and shrubs, which have little value to the owner. Real wood has value, so taking it would be stealing.

phrases.english: "And they may gather wood from their fields."
We said this only about thorns and shrubs,
but with other kinds of wood, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְלַקְּטִין עֵצִים מִשְּׂדוֹתֵיהֶם. לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בְּהִיזְמֵי וְהִיגֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first condition (grazing) to the second (gathering wood), using the same limiting style.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wood-gathering right covers only thorns and shrubs, not other wood.

steps.title: Only thorns still attached to the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a second limit: even thorns and shrubs may be taken only while still growing in the ground. Once the owner has cut them, they may not be taken.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even with thorns and shrubs, we said this only when they are attached to the ground, but when they are cut off, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the wood-gathering right one more step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner has already cut the thorns, he has shown he wants them for himself, so they are now his and taking them would be stealing. The right only covers what is still growing and unclaimed. The next step narrows the rule even further.

keyTerms.meaning: Attached to the ground, still growing

phrases.english: And even with thorns and shrubs,
we said this only when they are attached to the ground,
but when they are detached, no.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּהִיזְמֵי וְהִיגֵי לָא אֲמַרַן אֶלָּא בִּמְחוּבָּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second limit on top of the limit in the previous step.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even thorns and shrubs may be gathered only while still attached to the ground, not after the owner has cut them.

steps.title: Only moist growth, and never pulling out the roots
steps.stepSummary: Even attached thorns and shrubs may be taken only while moist, not when dry. They also may never be pulled up by the roots.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even when they are still attached, we only allow moist ones, not dry ones. And he may not pull them out by the roots.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds two more limits to the right to gather wood: the growth must be moist, and the gatherer may not uproot it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 5 allowed only attached thorns and shrubs. Now even attached ones are allowed only while moist, because dry wood is useful to the owner as firewood. Pulling out the roots is also forbidden, so the gatherer may only cut or snap off the top.
steps.whatToRemember: The public may take only thorns and shrubs that are still attached and moist, and only without uprooting them.

phrases.english: And even with attached ones,
phrases.notes: This picks up from step 5, which allowed only thorns and shrubs still growing in the ground.

phrases.english: we only said this about moist ones,
but dry ones, no.
And only as long as he does not pull them out by the roots.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third and fourth limit to the wood-gathering right after steps 4 and 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only attached, moist thorns and shrubs may be taken, and they may not be uprooted.

steps.title: Quoting the rule about gathering wild grasses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next condition: wild grasses may be gathered anywhere except a תלתן field.
steps.simpleTranslation: And people may gather wild grasses anywhere, except from a field of fenugreek.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the ברייתא to set up a question about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line was already listed in step 1. Here the גמרא brings it again because it is about to ask what the exception for תלתן tells us.

keyTerms.meaning: Fenugreek, a plant grown for seeds, stalks or fodder

phrases.english: And people may gather wild grasses in any place,
except from a fenugreek field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wood condition to the next condition in the ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Wild grasses may be gathered anywhere except from a תלתן field.

steps.title: Are grasses good or bad for fenugreek?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests grasses help תלתן. A משנה in כלאים suggests grasses harm it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does this mean grasses are good for fenugreek? But there is a contradiction: if fenugreek came up together with wild grasses, the owner does not have to uproot them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from the ברייתא and then challenges it with a משנה that seems to say the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner wants the grasses left in his תלתן field, they must be good for it. But the משנה about כלאים does not require uprooting grasses that grow with תלתן. That only makes sense if the grasses harm it, since harmful growth is not treated as planting mixed crops.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say...? Drawing a conclusion
And they pointed out a contradiction

phrases.english: Is this to say that grasses are good for fenugreek?
But a contradiction was raised:
Fenugreek that came up together with kinds of wild grasses,
we do not require him to uproot them!
phrases.notes: This is from a משנה about mixed planting. The grasses can stay because they hurt the fenugreek, so it doesn't count as growing them together.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the quoted ברייתא and challenges it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference from the ברייתא that grasses are good for תלתן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה in כלאים treats grasses as harmful to תלתן, which contradicts the idea that they help it.

steps.title: Grown for seed versus grown for stalks
steps.stepSummary: רב ירמיה says that grasses harm תלתן grown for seed but help תלתן grown for stalks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ירמיה said: There is no problem. One source is about fenugreek grown for its seeds, the other about fenugreek grown for its stalks. For seeds, grasses are bad because they weaken it. For stalks, grasses are good because the plant climbs on them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ירמיה answers the contradiction by saying the two sources are talking about two different kinds of תלתן fields.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is about תלתן grown for seed, where grasses weaken the plant. The ברייתא is about תלתן grown for stalks, where grasses help the plant climb and grow bigger. So the owner wants the grasses left only in a stalk field.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; there is no contradiction

phrases.english: רב ירמיה said: It is not difficult;
here it is grown for seeds, there it is grown for stalks.
For seeds, grasses are bad for it,
because they weaken it;
for stalks, they are good for it,
because when it stands among grasses, it climbs on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה לָא קַשְׁיָא כָּאן לְזֶרַע כָּאן לְזִירִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is about a different type of field
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Grasses must be either always good or always bad for תלתן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Grasses harm תלתן grown for seed and help תלתן grown for stalks.

steps.title: Grown for people versus grown for animals
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the משנה is about תלתן grown for people, and the ברייתא is about תלתן grown for animal feed, where the owner wants the grasses too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you prefer, say: one source is about fenugreek grown for people, the other about fenugreek grown for animals. Since he planted it for animals, he wants the grasses too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to the same contradiction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the difference is not about whether grasses help the plant. If the owner grows תלתן to feed animals, the grasses are also animal food, so he wants them and the public may not take them. In a field grown for people, the grasses are only a nuisance.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say: introduces another answer

steps.confusionAlert: This answer does not say grasses help the plant grow. It says the owner wants the grasses themselves as animal food.

phrases.english: If you wish, say:
here it is grown for people, there it is grown for animals.
For since he planted it for animals,
he needs the grasses too.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא כָּאן לְאָדָם כָּאן לִבְהֵמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the contradiction in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases by the purpose of the field
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The exception in the ברייתא must mean grasses help תלתן grow.
steps.terutzMaskana: In an animal-feed field the owner wants the grasses as fodder, so the public may not take them.

steps.title: How can we tell what the field is for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how an outsider can know whether a תלתן field was planted for people or for animals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about the second answer and sets up רב פפא's reply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone gathering grasses cannot ask the owner what he planned. The second answer only works if there is a visible sign that shows the purpose of the field.

phrases.english: And how do we know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to apply the answer in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A visible sign that shows whether a תלתן field was planted for people or for animals.

steps.title: Rows mean people, no rows mean animals
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא says that a field planted in rows is for people, and a field not planted in rows is for animals.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: If he planted it in rows, it is for people. If he did not plant it in rows, it is for animals.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a simple sign to tell which kind of תלתן field it is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Planting in neat rows shows care, which fits food for people. Scattered planting fits animal feed, so in such a field the grasses belong to the owner and may not be gathered.
steps.whatToRemember: Grasses may be gathered from a תלתן field only when the owner does not want them: either it is grown for seed (רב ירמיה), or it is grown for people, which you can tell by its rows (רב פפא).

phrases.english: רב פפא said:
If he planted it in rows, it is for people;
if he did not plant it in rows, it is for animals.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא שָׁארְיָה מְשָׁארֵי לְאָדָם
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Rows show the field is for people. No rows show it is for animals.

steps.title: Anyone may cut a shoot for planting, except from an olive tree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next condition from the ברייתא: people may cut young shoots from anyone's tree to plant, except shoots of an olive tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: And people may cut off a shoot anywhere to plant it, except for olive shoots.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the list of conditions in the ברייתא and quotes the next one. It allows cutting shoots from another person's tree for planting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the גמרא was discussing the condition about grasses in a תלתן field. Now it moves to a new condition. Cutting a shoot costs the owner very little and helps someone else plant, so it was allowed. Olive trees are left out because cutting their shoots would cause the tree real harm.

keyTerms.meaning: they cut off or pluck off (a small branch)
a young shoot or sapling used for planting
shoots that grow from the trunk or base of a tree

phrases.english: And one may cut off a shoot anywhere,
phrases.notes: This is the next item in the list of conditions יהושע made when the land was divided. 'Anywhere' means even from someone else's tree.

phrases.english: except for olive shoots.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The discussion of the תלתן condition is finished, and the ברייתא's list moves on to a new condition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Anyone may cut shoots from another person's tree for planting, except olive shoots.

steps.title: How much may be taken from olives, reeds, vines and other trees
steps.stepSummary: An elder, quoted by רבי תנחום and רבי ברייס, explains the limits. For olive trees the measure is the size of an egg. For reeds and vines, shoots are taken only from the first knot and up. For other trees, they are taken from the thick part and not the thin part.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי תנחום and רבי ברייס explained in the name of a certain elder: for an olive tree, the measure is the size of an egg. For reeds and grapevines, one may take from the knot and higher. For all other trees, one may take from the thick part of the tree, not from its thin tip.
steps.whatsHappening: An elder explains how the shoot-cutting rule actually works for each kind of plant. The details limit the permission so the owner's tree is not hurt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave a general permission with one exception. Now each kind of plant gets its own limit. For an olive tree, an egg-sized piece is left on the trunk. For reeds and vines, the cut must be above the first knot so the plant can keep growing. For other trees, the cut must come from the thick, crowded part, where losing a branch matters less.

keyTerms.meaning: a certain elder (a sage whose name is not given)
a knot or joint on a reed or vine
the thick part of the tree, where many branches grow
the thin, pointed part of the tree

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two olive rules. The ברייתא's exception is for גרופיות, the stumps left when an olive tree is cut down. רש״י says no shoot may be cut from them at all, because that damages the stumps. The elder's egg-size measure is about cutting from an olive tree in general, which is allowed within that limit.

phrases.english: Rabbi Tanchum and Rabbi Berayes explained
in the name of a certain elder:
With an olive tree – the size of an egg.
phrases.notes: He means one must leave an egg-sized piece on the trunk when cutting the shoot from an olive tree.

phrases.english: With reeds and grapevines –
from the knot and higher.
phrases.notes: This is the first knot on the stalk, so the cut is made above it.

phrases.english: And all other trees –
from the thick part of the tree,
and not from the thin part of the tree;

steps.triggerLanguage: פֵּירְשׁוּ רַבִּי תַּנְחוּם וְרַבִּי בִּרְיָיס מִשּׁוּם זָקֵן אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains and limits the general permission to cut shoots given in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Olive: an egg-sized measure. Reeds and vines: from the first knot and up. Other trees: from the thick part only.

steps.title: Take from young branches and from the shaded side
steps.stepSummary: The elder adds more limits. Shoots must come from new branches that do not yet give fruit, not old fruit-bearing ones. They must also come from a part of the tree that does not face the sun. His list continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: One may take from a new branch that does not produce fruit, but not from an old branch that does produce fruit; and from a place that does not see the sun,
steps.whatsHappening: The elder keeps going with his list. Now he tells us which branches on the tree may be cut, and the list is still not finished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last step was about which kind of plant and which area of it. Now the rule picks the branch by its age and its place. Old branches already give fruit and sunny spots grow the best fruit, so taking from them would cost the owner. A young branch or a shaded one is worth less to him, so taking it is allowed.

phrases.english: From a new branch, which does not produce fruit,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא מִן יָשָׁן שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה פֵּירוֹת;
phrases.english: and not from an old branch, which does produce fruit;
from a place that does not face the sun,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the elder's explanation from step 14 with more limits on which branches may be cut.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Shoots are taken from new branches that do not yet give fruit, not from old fruit-bearing ones, and from a place that does not face the sun.
